name: Glutathione injections
lead: Glutathione (GSH) is a small tripeptide made of glutamate, cysteine and glycine that cells produce naturally and use as a major antioxidant [1]. Intravenous or intramuscular glutathione is promoted in some countries and online communities as a skin-lightening and "glow" treatment, often alongside vitamin C, with the aim of a lighter, more even complexion, fewer dark patches and a brighter look [2][9].

The appearance chain proponents describe runs from injected glutathione, to reduced melanin production, to lighter skin tone. A 2016 review in the Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology described the proposed mechanism as direct and indirect inhibition of the enzyme tyrosinase and a shift from dark eumelanin to lighter phaeomelanin production [10][14].

Reference works state that whether glutathione actually lightens skin was unclear as of 2019, citing a systematic review, and that the Philippine government recommends against intravenous glutathione because of possible side effects [2][11]. The 2016 review describes a gap between evidence for efficacy and for safety, and reports that randomized trials supporting a lightening effect involved oral and topical forms rather than injections [10][14]. In 2026 US compounding pharmacies recalled injectable glutathione lots for elevated bacterial endotoxin, an episode that drew media attention to the practice [7].

paras: Glutathione is built from glutamate, cysteine and glycine, with cysteine joined through an unusual gamma linkage that helps resist peptide breakdown. In healthy cells more than 90 percent of the pool is in the reduced form, and intracellular concentrations are far higher than extracellular ones.[1]

It neutralises reactive oxygen species, supports enzymes such as glutathione peroxidases, helps keep vitamins C and E in their active forms, and conjugates reactive metabolites such as the toxic acetaminophen metabolite NAPQI.[1] The reference article notes that oral glutathione is poorly absorbed systemically, because digestive proteases break it down.[1]

Glutathione is described as the most common agent taken by mouth to lighten skin, and it is also used in creams [2]. Intravenous and intramuscular forms are used in clinics and spa settings, frequently marketed in drips that pair glutathione with vitamin C for a brighter or even complexion [2][8]. The 2016 review notes that its promotion for this purpose is widespread in some ethnic populations and that intravenous use is popular [10].

Proponents of injection say it bypasses the poor oral absorption of glutathione and raises levels more reliably than capsules [1][2]. News coverage from India describes IV drips sought for a 'bridal glow' before weddings [8]. Marketing of injectable glutathione for skin lightening, detoxification, immune support and antioxidant effects is described in coverage of the 2026 recalls [7].

The 2016 review describes glutathione as a thiol tripeptide that maintains intracellular redox balance and notes that its antimelanogenic properties led to its promotion as a skin-lightening agent [10]. It reports that the lightening effect is attributed to direct and indirect inhibition of tyrosinase and to switching melanin synthesis from eumelanin to phaeomelanin [14]. The authors note that treatment duration, how long any effect lasts and maintenance protocols remain unclear and call for larger, long-term, double-blind placebo-controlled trials [14].

The 2016 review of glutathione as a skin-whitening agent weighs the available evidence and controversies and describes a dichotomy between evidence for efficacy and for safety; it reports that three randomized controlled trials support a lightening effect and good safety for topical and oral glutathione, while describing intravenous glutathione as popular but without evidence proving its efficacy [10][14].

A 2019 systematic review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology searched databases through October 2017 and found four studies in healthy volunteers, three of them placebo-controlled randomized trials. Oral glutathione at 500 mg per day and a topical 2.0 percent oxidized glutathione product appeared to lighten sun-exposed skin by melanin index, with no significant change in sun-protected skin, and adverse events were not serious. The authors concluded that evidence of a skin whitening effect remained inconclusive, limited by study quality and inconsistent findings [11].

A 2021 double-blind Indonesian multicentre trial gave 83 participants aged 33 to 50 an oral supplement containing glutathione with ascorbic acid, alpha-lipoic acid and zinc aspartate, or placebo, for 12 weeks. Skin measures improved more in the supplement group, but the differences were not statistically significant overall, and side effects in both groups were mild and temporary [12].

Recent reviews have widened the picture. A 2025 PRISMA-guided systematic review of five clinical trials of topical glutathione reported that a 2 percent oxidized glutathione lotion lowered the melanin index, with limited safety data. A 2026 systematic review of 194 studies reported that topical and oral glutathione improved pigmentation and brightness, and that injectable glutathione raises systemic levels quickly but with short-lived effects and safety concerns. A 2025 narrative review described oral glutathione as giving variable melanin reduction with few side effects, and intravenous glutathione as fast acting but associated with serious risks and lacking standardized dosing [13].

No studies found of injected glutathione for general skin lightening in healthy people. One registered trial (NCT07595705) is testing a vitamin C and glutathione approach for gingival hyperpigmentation, which concerns gum tissue and is not a study of skin lightening; it is recruiting [3]. A trial of a multi-ingredient injectable (NCT07929870) listing skin pigmentation among its outcomes has not started recruiting [4].
Related research includes animal studies of glutathione injection, for example in mice exposed to radiation and in rats with peritonitis, which are not studies of appearance [5][6].

The 2016 review states that adverse effects of intravenous glutathione led the Philippine Food and Drug Administration to issue an advisory against off-label use for skin lightening, and Wikipedia reports that the Philippine government recommends against IV glutathione because of possible side effects [10][2][14]. The 2025 narrative review lists anaphylaxis and liver toxicity among reported serious risks of intravenous use [13].

In 2026 Victory Medical Center Pharmacy of Austin recalled three lots of compounded glutathione, and Optimal Balance Pharmacy of Houston recalled one lot of 200 mg/mL multi-dose vials in fourteen states after testing found elevated bacterial endotoxin. Medical Daily reports that the company received reports of fever, chills, severe headache, nausea, vomiting and allergic-type symptoms; that the FDA's published risk statement says high-endotoxin injectables could cause serious events including low blood pressure, anaphylactic shock and death; and that the FDA has not approved any injectable glutathione for safety or effectiveness [7].

The same report notes that the FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality, that most compounding pharmacies are overseen mainly by state pharmacy boards, and that in 2019 the FDA warned a compounder about using supplement-grade ingredients to make sterile glutathione injections. A Texas woman has sued the Austin pharmacy, alleging hospitalization after an infusion; these are unproven allegations [7]. A 2026 Times of India article headlined that doctors flag health risks of IV drips sought for a bridal glow [8].

On looksmax.org, glutathione IV is discussed as a way to lighten skin tone and clear undertones, often by users reasoning from its status as the body's main antioxidant. One thread asks whether injections clear undertones, and one user reports an IV session after which his eyes looked lighter [9].

card.summary: Injected glutathione is used for skin lightening, but its effectiveness is unclear and the Philippine government advises against IV use.
card.note: Philippine government recommends against intravenous glutathione; efficacy unclear as of a 2019 review.

quick.overview:
Glutathione is an antioxidant peptide the body makes. Some clinics and online communities use injections or IV drips of it to lighten skin.

Reference works describe its effectiveness for skin whitening as unclear as of 2019. No controlled trial of injected glutathione for general skin lightening was found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say glutathione reduces melanin production, and that injection avoids poor oral absorption. Reference sources confirm oral absorption is poor but do not establish the lightening mechanism.
quick.risks: The Philippine government recommends against intravenous glutathione because of possible side effects. No controlled safety data for cosmetic injection were found.

angle.text: Injected glutathione is used by people who want lighter or brighter skin and fewer dark patches. The proposed route is reduced melanin synthesis, which proponents say injection delivers better than oral forms. Some forum users also discuss it for brighter eyes and clearer undertones.
